lesson.title: Linear Combination: Scaling Equations Before You Combine Them
lesson.summary: A linear combination scales one or both equations in a system by chosen constants before adding them, generalizing the elimination method so it works even when no variable's coefficients start out as opposites.
lesson.body:
Multiplying both sides of a true equation by the same nonzero constant produces another true equation describing the exact same line; the equation looks different, but nothing about its solutions has changed. A linear combination puts this fact to work on an entire system: multiply each equation in the system by a chosen constant, then add the results together. The new equation produced this way is still guaranteed to be true for any solution of the original system, and by choosing the constants carefully, one of the variables can be made to cancel out completely, no matter what its original coefficients were.

This is exactly the generalized version of the elimination method from the previous section. Basic elimination worked whenever a variable's coefficients already happened to be opposites, letting simple addition cancel that variable. Linear combination handles the general case by first finding a common multiple of that variable's two coefficients, the same least-common-multiple reasoning used elsewhere in algebra, and scaling each equation so the coefficients become opposites before adding. In this sense, plain elimination is just a linear combination where both scaling constants happen to already be 1.

Consider the system 2x + 3y = 12 and 5x - 2y = 11. Neither variable has matching or opposite coefficients yet. To eliminate y, look at its coefficients, 3 and -2, and find a common multiple: 6 works, since 3 times 2 is 6 and 2 times 3 is 6. Multiply the first equation by 2: 4x + 6y = 24. Multiply the second equation by 3: 15x - 6y = 33. Now the y-coefficients, +6 and -6, are opposites. Adding the two new equations: (4x + 6y) + (15x - 6y) = 24 + 33, which simplifies to 19x = 57, so x = 3.

Substitute x = 3 back into the original first equation: 2(3) + 3y = 12, so 6 + 3y = 12, giving 3y = 6, so y = 2. The candidate solution is (3, 2). Check it in the original second equation: 5(3) - 2(2) = 15 - 4 = 11, which matches. Check the original first equation: 2(3) + 3(2) = 6 + 6 = 12, which also matches. The solution (3, 2) is confirmed for the original system, and because the scaling only multiplied each equation by a nonzero constant, the scaled equations describe the same two lines as the originals, so solving the scaled system is guaranteed to give the same answer.

Because a linear combination can be built to eliminate either variable, whichever is arithmetically simpler, this technique gives full control over how to attack any linear system, and it works exactly as reliably for revealing inconsistent systems, through a false statement, or dependent systems, through an identity, as the simpler elimination cases already have. It is, in effect, the complete and general version of the elimination idea, and it is the method that scales up most naturally to systems with three or more variables in later courses.
